title: Speed round: one awk vs. a pipeline
briefing: The incident commander wants two numbers for the web tier: how many 404s the server sent during the recon day, and how many different clients received them. You could answer with a five-stage pipeline, or with one `awk`.
Get the answer both ways and time them. Then decide which one you would put in a script.

lesson.p: Every stage of a pipeline is a separate process reading the whole stream. `awk` can filter, extract, count, and de-duplicate in one pass. Neither is always better: a pipeline is easy to build one stage at a time, and one awk is easier to run over a huge file.

flags: bash's built-in timer: real (wall clock), user and sys (CPU) time for the whole pipeline. It prints to stderr.
awk idiom: true the FIRST time a value is seen, false after. Unique values without sorting.
count per key in one pass: the awk form of `sort | uniq -c`
count distinct values while doing other work on the same line
the pipeline form: three processes, and `sort` has to read everything before it prints anything

lesson.code:
time (cut -d' ' -f1 var/log/httpd/access_log.1 | sort -u | wc -l)
time awk '!seen[$1]++ {n++} END {print n}' var/log/httpd/access_log.1

lesson.note: In this VM the awk version is about three times faster on access_log.1, mostly because it starts one process instead of three and never sorts. On a real 2 GB log the gap grows: `sort` needs memory and temporary files, and awk only keeps one array entry per distinct key. Time it on your data; do not assume.

examples.title: Distinct values: pipeline vs. awk
examples.command: cut -d' ' -f1 training/web.log | sort -u | wc -l; awk '!seen[$1]++ {n++} END {print n}' training/web.log

stages.why: Three processes: extract, sort and de-duplicate, count.
One process. `seen[$1]++` is 0 (false) the first time an IP appears, so `!` makes it true exactly once per IP.
With no action, awk prints the line: the first request from each IP, in the order they arrived. `sort -u` cannot keep that order.
The Level 4 counting pipeline on the status column.

examples.title: Counts per key: one awk
examples.command: awk '{c[$9]++} END {for (s in c) print c[s], s}' training/web.log | sort -k2

stages.why: One counter per status code, in a single pass.

stages.code: END {for (s in c) print c[s], s} | sort -k2
stages.why: Print count then key, like `uniq -c`, sorted by key. Same numbers as the pipeline.

challenge.question: In var/log/httpd/access_log.1, how many responses had status 404, and how many distinct client IPs received at least one 404?
challenge.format: The two numbers separated by one space, count first, for example 120 9

hints: The status is field 9 and the client IP is field 1 (split on spaces). Count the lines where field 9 is 404, and count the different IPs on those lines.
One awk can do both in one pass: on lines where `$9 == 404`, add 1 to a counter, and add 1 to a second counter the first time each `$1` is seen (`if (!seen[$1]++)`). Print both in END.
awk '$9 == 404 {n++; if (!seen[$1]++) ips++} END {print n, ___}' var/log/httpd/access_log.1

debrief.solution: awk '$9 == 404 {n++; if (!seen[$1]++) ips++} END {print n, ips}' var/log/httpd/access_log.1
debrief.alternative: f=var/log/httpd/access_log.1; echo $(cut -d' ' -f9 $f | grep -cx 404) $(cut -d' ' -f1,9 $f | grep ' 404$' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort -u | wc -l)
why: 201 404s, spread across 15 clients, but one client accounts for 51 of them: the scanner, 203.0.113.66 (`awk '$9 == 404 {print $1}' var/log/httpd/access_log.1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -3`). A raw 404 count is a weak alert on its own; 404s per client over a short window is the signal that catches a scanner.

The pipeline reads the file twice and starts seven processes; the awk reads it once and starts one. For a one-off question that difference rarely matters. For a cron job or a monitoring check that runs every minute over a growing log, it does.

Write whichever version the next person can read. A pipeline you built stage by stage is easy to debug; an awk program with three arrays is not. When an awk one-liner grows past a line, put it in a file (`awk -f report.awk`) with a comment per block.
